entries.title: Bread pudding soufflé
entries.summary: Commander's Palace's signature: New Orleans bread pudding folded into meringue and baked tall in a ramekin, with whiskey sauce poured into its centre at the table. It marries a set bread custard to a soufflé, and Brennan's does not serve it.
entries.guest: The bread pudding soufflé is the famous dessert of Commander's Palace, run by another branch of the Brennan family. Ours is the New Orleans Bread Pudding, with whiskey caramel and pralines.

paras: A bread pudding soufflé is New Orleans bread pudding broken up, folded through whipped egg white and baked in a ramekin, a small straight-sided dish, until it rises tall above the rim. It is the signature dessert of Commander's Palace in the Garden District, where the server opens the top at the table and pours whiskey sauce into the centre. Guests ask for it by name at the wrong house.

It marries two techniques. Bread pudding is a set bread custard: bread soaked in sweet custard and baked until the egg sets. A soufflé, French for puffed, is a flavoured base lightened with meringue, egg white whipped with sugar; here the broken pudding is the base. In the oven the air expands, water turns to steam and the egg white sets round the bubbles. The pudding brings flavour and body; the meringue brings lift.

Bake the bread pudding first: cubes of light New Orleans French bread soaked in eggs, cream, sugar, vanilla and spice, baked at 180°C (356°F) for 30 to 40 minutes in a shallow pan, until set at the centre, about 80°C (176°F) on a probe. Cool it completely, because a warm, wet pudding melts the meringue and sinks the rise.

Brush the ramekins with soft butter in upward strokes and coat them with sugar: the soufflé climbs the walls on that grip. In a spotless bowl with no trace of yolk or fat, whip the whites with a pinch of cream of tartar, a powdered acid that steadies the foam, adding the sugar a spoonful at a time, to firm, glossy peaks that bend slightly at the tip, never dry and grainy.

Break the cold pudding into small pieces and stir in a quarter of the meringue to loosen it. Fold in the rest in two additions: cut down through the middle with a large spatula, sweep along the bottom and up the side, turn the bowl and repeat, stopping once the white streaks are gone. Fill the ramekins to the rim, wipe the rims and run a thumb round the inside edge so the top rises straight. Bake at 180°C (356°F) for 15 to 20 minutes, the door shut for the first ten.

It is ready with straight sides, a rise of about 2.5 cm (1 inch) above the rim, a golden top and a gentle wobble when nudged. It falls as it cools, so it goes straight to the table. Many restaurant versions thicken cream with cornflour (cornstarch) mixed smooth in cold water, a slurry, then sweeten it and finish it with bourbon; the older New Orleans whiskey sauce is butter, sugar and egg.

A flat, dense soufflé means underwhipped meringue, heavy folding or a trace of fat in the bowl. A lopsided rise comes from patchy butter, mix on the rim or a hot spot in the oven. A grainy meringue that weeps beads of syrup had its sugar added too fast or was whipped past glossy. A wet layer at the bottom means the pudding was underbaked or still warm. One that sinks before the table was underbaked or waited at the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen: fire it to the guest's pace.

Brennan's does not serve a bread pudding soufflé. Its dessert is the New Orleans Bread Pudding: bread pudding with a warm whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream for tang and pralines for crunch. Mention the whiskey to a guest who avoids alcohol.

Guests mix the houses up because both carry the Brennan name. Owen Brennan opened in 1946, and the restaurant has been at 417 Royal Street since 1956. The family split in 1973, settled in 1974: Owen's widow and sons kept Royal Street, and Ella Brennan's side took Commander's Palace. Brennan's closed in 2013 and reopened in November 2014 under Ralph Brennan, a cousin, and his partner Terry White; the two houses are separate businesses.

When a guest asks for the bread pudding soufflé, never correct them sharply; it is an easy mistake. Say it is the famous dessert at Commander's Palace, run by another branch of the Brennan family, and offer ours. Allergy and dietary questions about any dessert go to the service note and the kitchen.

ratios.label: Whites to sugar in the meringue
ratios.value: About 9 egg whites to 150 g (3/4 cup) sugar for six ramekins

ratios.label: Broken pudding to meringue
ratios.value: Roughly equal volumes, folded until no white streaks remain

ratios.label: Whiskey sauce, one working version
ratios.value: 350 ml (1 1/2 cups) cream, 15 ml (1 tbsp) cornflour slaked in 45 ml (3 tbsp) water, 70 g (1/3 cup) sugar, bourbon to taste

temps.label: Bake the bread pudding, then the soufflé
The bread pudding custard is set at the centre

faults.cause: Underwhipped meringue, heavy folding, or a trace of fat or yolk in the bowl.
faults.fix: Whip clean whites to firm, glossy peaks and fold gently, stopping once the streaks are gone.

faults.cause: Patchy butter on the ramekin, mix on the rim or a hot spot in the oven.
faults.fix: Butter in upward strokes, sugar evenly, wipe the rim and run a thumb round the edge.

faults.fault: Grainy meringue or beads of syrup
faults.cause: Sugar added too fast, or whites whipped past glossy to dry.
faults.fix: Add the sugar a spoonful at a time and stop at firm, glossy peaks.

faults.fault: Wet, eggy layer at the bottom
faults.cause: The bread pudding was underbaked or still warm when the soufflé was built.
faults.fix: Bake the pudding until set at the centre and cool it completely first.

faults.fault: Sinks before it reaches the table
faults.cause: Underbaked, or left waiting at the pass.
faults.fix: Bake to the cues and fire it to the guest's pace, with a runner ready.

faults.cause: Cornflour added dry to hot cream.
faults.fix: Mix the cornflour smooth in cold water first, whisk it in and bring the sauce back to a simmer.

cards.front: What is a bread pudding soufflé?
cards.back: New Orleans bread pudding broken up and folded into meringue, baked in a ramekin until it rises tall, with whiskey sauce poured into its centre at the table.

cards.front: Which New Orleans restaurant has the bread pudding soufflé as its signature?
cards.back: Commander's Palace in the Garden District, run by a branch of the Brennan family as a separate business from Brennan's on Royal Street.

cards.front: Which two techniques does the bread pudding soufflé marry?
cards.back: A set bread custard, the bread pudding baked first, and a soufflé, lifted by meringue folded through the broken pudding.

cards.front: Why is the bread pudding baked and cooled before the soufflé is built?
cards.back: The set custard gives flavour and body, and a warm, wet pudding would melt the meringue and sink the rise.

cards.front: What makes a soufflé rise in the oven?
cards.back: Air whipped into the egg white expands and water in the mix turns to steam, then the egg white sets round the bubbles.

cards.front: To what stage are the whites whipped for the soufflé?
cards.back: Firm, glossy peaks that bend slightly at the tip, with the sugar added a spoonful at a time; dry, grainy whites will not fold smoothly.

cards.front: How is the meringue folded into the broken pudding?
cards.back: Loosen the pudding with a quarter of the meringue, then fold in the rest gently: down the middle, along the bottom, up the side, turning the bowl.

cards.front: Why is the ramekin buttered in upward strokes and coated with sugar?
cards.back: It gives the soufflé a grip to climb straight up the walls; a clean rim and a thumb run round the edge keep the rise even.

cards.front: What are the cues of a soufflé ready to serve?
cards.back: Straight sides, a rise of about 2.5 cm (1 inch) above the rim, a golden top and a gentle wobble. It goes to the table at once.

cards.front: How does the whiskey sauce reach the soufflé?
cards.back: At the table the server spoons a hole in the top and pours the whiskey sauce into the centre, in front of the guest.

cards.front: Why do guests confuse Commander's Palace with Brennan's on Royal Street?
cards.back: Both carry the Brennan name: Commander's Palace went to Ella Brennan's side of the family in the split of 1973, settled in 1974, and has been a separate business ever since.

cards.front: What do you offer a Brennan's guest who asks for the bread pudding soufflé?
cards.back: Our New Orleans Bread Pudding, with a warm whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream and pralines. Mention the whiskey to a guest who avoids alcohol.

questions.q: Which restaurant is known for the bread pudding soufflé?
distractors: Antoine's
Galatoire's
Brennan's on Royal Street
questions.why: The soufflé is the signature of Commander's Palace in the Garden District; Brennan's on Royal Street serves a New Orleans Bread Pudding instead.

questions.q: Why is the bread pudding baked and cooled before the soufflé is built?
distractors: Raw custard rises higher in the oven
Baking it twice burns off the spice
So the bread soaks up more meringue
questions.why: The set, cold pudding brings body and flavour without melting the meringue, so the soufflé keeps the air that lifts it.

questions.q: What lifts a bread pudding soufflé as it bakes?
questions.answer: Air and steam held by egg white
distractors: Baking powder stirred into the custard
Yeast still proving in the bread
Whipped cream folded through the pudding
questions.why: The whipped whites trap air that expands with heat while water turns to steam; the egg white then sets round the bubbles.

questions.q: To what stage should the whites be whipped for the soufflé?
questions.answer: Firm, glossy peaks with a slight bend
distractors: A loose foam that barely holds
Dry, grainy and broken into clumps
Until stiff enough to cut with a knife
questions.why: Firm, glossy whites fold in smoothly and hold their air; underwhipped whites give little lift, and dry ones break into lumps.

questions.q: What is the first step in folding the meringue into the broken pudding?
questions.answer: Stir in a quarter of the meringue
distractors: Beat all the meringue in hard with a whisk
Drop the pudding onto the meringue in one lump
Blend the two together until smooth
questions.why: A little meringue lightens the heavy pudding first, so the rest can be folded in gently without knocking out its air.

questions.q: Why is the ramekin buttered in upward strokes and coated with sugar?
questions.answer: So the soufflé climbs straight up
distractors: So the soufflé tastes of caramel
So the ramekin can be chilled overnight
So the sauce cannot soak in
questions.why: The butter and sugar give the rising mix a grip on the walls, so it climbs evenly instead of sticking or leaning.

questions.q: Which of these tells you a soufflé is ready to serve?
questions.answer: It has risen straight above the rim
distractors: It has sunk level with the rim
Its top has cracked and darkened
It is firm and still when nudged
questions.why: A ready soufflé stands straight and tall above the rim with a golden top and a gentle wobble, and goes out at once.

questions.q: How does the whiskey sauce reach a bread pudding soufflé?
questions.answer: Poured into its centre at the table
distractors: Baked underneath it in the ramekin
Brushed over the top before baking
Served cold in a jug on the side for later
questions.why: The server opens the top with a spoon and pours the whiskey sauce into the centre in front of the guest, so it soaks the soufflé as it is eaten.

questions.q: Why do guests sometimes ask for the bread pudding soufflé at Brennan's on Royal Street?
questions.answer: Commander's is a Brennan family house too
distractors: Brennan's owns Commander's Palace
The soufflé was created on Royal Street
The two houses share one kitchen
questions.why: In the family split of 1973, settled in 1974, Commander's Palace went to Ella Brennan's side, so the shared name sends guests to the wrong house.

entries.title: Crêpes Suzette at the table
entries.summary: Thin crêpes warmed in beurre Suzette, a sauce of butter, sugar and orange, then flamed with orange liqueur and brandy. A founding flamed dessert whose origin is told in rival stories, still made at the table in the old New Orleans houses.
entries.guest: Crêpes Suzette are thin French pancakes warmed in butter, sugar and orange, then flamed with orange liqueur and brandy. Our flamed dessert is the Bananas Foster, made at your table.

paras: Crêpes Suzette are thin French pancakes warmed in beurre Suzette, a sauce of butter, sugar and orange juice and zest, then flamed with orange liqueur and brandy and served in their syrup. A crêpe (KRAYP) is a pancake of thin batter with no raising agent, cooked fast in a hot pan until supple and lacy. Still made at the table in the old New Orleans houses, it asks for three skills: thin crêpes, a glossy citrus syrup and a calm flame.

Whisk 125 g (1 cup) flour, a pinch of salt and a spoonful of sugar with 2 eggs, then whisk in 300 ml (1 1/4 cups) milk a little at a time, against lumps, and finish with 30 g (1 oz) melted butter. It should pour like thin cream. Rest it, covered and chilled, for at least an hour: the flour absorbs the liquid and the bubbles settle, so the crêpes come out thin and tender.

Heat an 18 to 20 cm (7 to 8 inch) crêpe pan over a medium-high flame and wipe it with clarified butter. Pour in about 45 ml (3 tbsp) of batter and tilt and swirl at once into a thin sheet. After about a minute the edges turn lacy and lift; turn it and give the second side 20 to 30 seconds. Allow three a guest.

For the sauce, melt butter and sugar in a wide pan until pale gold, add orange juice and zest, often with a little lemon, and reduce to a glossy syrup. Coat each crêpe on both sides, fold it into quarters with the prettier first-cooked side outward, and push it aside. Off the flame add orange liqueur, such as Grand Marnier, and brandy, usually Cognac; return the pan, tilt to light it, spoon the burning syrup over, and plate once the flame dies.

Crêpes Suzette heads a small family of flamed desserts. Cherries jubilee is generally credited to Escoffier for one of Queen Victoria's jubilees, most often said to be 1897: cherries in a thickened syrup, lit with kirsch, a clear cherry brandy. Bananas Foster, created at Brennan's in 1951, flames bananas in a caramel of butter, brown sugar and cinnamon with rum, and banana liqueur in the house's published recipe. Each is a hot syrup, a warmed spirit and a flame.

Thick, rubbery crêpes mean a batter too thick or unrested, or too much in the pan. Tears on turning mean a cool pan or a crêpe turned too soon. A bitter sauce had its sugar taken too dark, or pith came with the zest. A greasy, separated sauce boiled too hard: swirl in orange juice off the heat. Soggy crêpes sat too long in the syrup.

Nobody knows who first made it, so tell the stories as stories. The best known is Henri Charpentier's: in his memoir he said that in 1895, as an assistant waiter at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, he lit the sauce by accident while serving the Prince of Wales, later Edward VII, who named it for a young lady at his table, Suzette. Charpentier was then a teenager, and the Larousse Gastronomique doubts that a boy so young served a prince. Another story names a Paris actress known as Suzette who served crêpes on stage.

Escoffier's Guide Culinaire, in its 1907 English edition, A Guide to Modern Cookery, warms the crêpes in a butter of mandarin zest and juice, sugar and curaçao, an orange liqueur, with no flame at all: the flame came later, as tableside theatre. In New Orleans the old houses, Arnaud's among them, have long made crêpes Suzette at the table; menus change, so check a house's current menu before telling a guest it is served.

Crêpes Suzette is not on the Brennan's menu, but its family is. The World Famous Bananas Foster, created by the house in 1951, is flamed at the table on the guéridon, the tableside cart. Cherries Jubilee is flamed the same way, but it is not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026: confirm with a manager that it is served before offering it.

A guest who asks for crêpes Suzette here wants flame, orange and a little theatre: offer the Foster in the same terms. Flaming burns off some of the alcohol, never all, so say so to a guest who avoids alcohol. Say it KRAYP soo-ZET; KREP, nearer the French, is also heard.

ratios.label: Crêpe batter
ratios.value: 125 g (1 cup) flour, 2 eggs, 300 ml (1 1/4 cups) milk and 30 g (1 oz) melted butter

ratios.label: Batter in the pan
ratios.value: About 45 ml (3 tbsp) for an 18 to 20 cm (7 to 8 inch) pan

ratios.label: Beurre Suzette
ratios.value: 100 g (3.5 oz) butter, 100 g (1/2 cup) sugar, the zest of 2 oranges and the juice of 1 or 2

ratios.label: Spirit for two portions
ratios.value: About 30 ml (1 oz) each of orange liqueur and brandy

faults.cause: Batter too thick or unrested, or too much batter in the pan.
faults.fix: Thin the batter with milk until it pours like thin cream, rest it, and pour less, swirling at once.

faults.cause: The milk went in all at once.
faults.fix: Whisk the milk in a little at a time; strain a lumpy batter and rest it.

faults.fault: Tears as the crêpe is turned
faults.cause: Pan too cool, batter unrested, or the crêpe turned too soon.
faults.fix: Heat the pan properly and wait until the edges lift and turn lacy.

faults.cause: The pan was not hot or greased enough.
faults.fix: Heat the pan well and wipe it with clarified butter before each crêpe.

faults.cause: The butter and sugar went too dark, or pith came with the zest.
faults.fix: Take the butter and sugar only to pale gold, and grate the coloured zest alone.
Swirl in a splash of orange juice off the heat to bring it back together.

faults.cause: Left too long in the syrup.
faults.fix: Coat, fold, flame and serve; the crêpes only need warming through.

brennans.how: Crêpes Suzette is not on our menu, but the Foster is its cousin: flamed on the guéridon, the tableside cart, by steps every server learns word for word, the spirit measured first and added off the flame.

Cherries Jubilee, black cherries in a Luxardo sauce, from the Italian house known for maraschino cherries and liqueur, flamed at the table over vanilla ice cream, is the other cousin; it is not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026, so confirm with a manager first.

cards.front: What are crêpes Suzette?
cards.back: Thin crêpes warmed in beurre Suzette, a butter, sugar and orange sauce, then flamed with orange liqueur and brandy and served in the syrup.

cards.front: What is beurre Suzette?
cards.back: Butter with sugar and orange zest and juice, often with a little lemon, melted and reduced to a glossy syrup that warms the crêpes.

cards.front: Why is crêpe batter rested before it is cooked?
cards.back: The flour absorbs the liquid and the bubbles settle, so the crêpes come out tender, thin and less likely to tear.

cards.front: What is a working ratio for crêpe batter?
cards.back: About 125 g (1 cup) flour, 2 eggs and 300 ml (1 1/4 cups) milk, with 30 g (1 oz) melted butter; it pours like thin cream.

cards.front: How do you cook a thin, lacy crêpe?
cards.back: A hot pan wiped with clarified butter, about 45 ml (3 tbsp) of batter swirled at once to the edges, turned when the edges lift and lace.

cards.front: How are the crêpes folded in the sauce?
cards.back: Coated on both sides, folded in half and in half again with the prettier first-cooked side outward, then pushed aside for the flame.

cards.front: Which spirits flame classic crêpes Suzette?
cards.back: An orange liqueur, such as Grand Marnier or Cointreau, with brandy, usually Cognac, measured first, added off the flame and then lit.

cards.front: What is Henri Charpentier's story of crêpes Suzette?
cards.back: He said that in 1895, at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, he lit the sauce by accident serving the Prince of Wales, who named it for Suzette.

cards.front: Why is Charpentier's story told as a story, not a fact?
cards.back: Charpentier was then a teenage assistant waiter, and the Larousse Gastronomique doubts that he, rather than a senior waiter, served the prince; another story credits an actress known as Suzette.

cards.front: Where in New Orleans are crêpes Suzette made at the table?
cards.back: In the old houses, Arnaud's among them, as a dessert flamed at the table; menus change, so check a house's current menu before telling a guest it is served.

cards.front: Name the three classic flamed desserts of this family.
cards.back: Crêpes Suzette with orange liqueur and brandy, cherries jubilee with kirsch, and Bananas Foster with rum and, in the published recipe, banana liqueur, created at Brennan's in 1951.

cards.front: What do you offer a Brennan's guest who asks for crêpes Suzette?
cards.back: The Bananas Foster, flamed at the table on the guéridon; Cherries Jubilee only once a manager confirms it is being served. Flaming leaves some alcohol in the sauce: say so to a guest who avoids it.

questions.q: What goes into beurre Suzette, the sauce that warms the crêpes?
distractors: Butter, flour and hot milk
Cream, egg yolks and vanilla
Brown sugar, cinnamon and rum
questions.why: Beurre Suzette is butter and sugar with orange juice and zest, reduced to a glossy syrup; cinnamon and rum belong to the Foster.

questions.q: Why is crêpe batter rested before it is cooked?
questions.answer: So the crêpes are tender and tear less
distractors: So the batter ferments and rises like bread
So the eggs set before cooking
So the butter floats to the top
questions.why: Resting lets the flour absorb the liquid and the bubbles settle, giving thin, tender crêpes that hold together in the pan.

questions.q: When is a crêpe ready to be turned?
questions.answer: When the edges lift and turn lacy
distractors: As soon as the batter meets the pan
When the top has puffed and cracked
After five minutes on the first side
questions.why: After about a minute in a hot pan the edges lace and lift and the underside is golden in spots; turned sooner, it tears.

questions.q: Which pair of spirits flames classic crêpes Suzette?
distractors: Dark rum and banana liqueur
Kirsch and maraschino
Bourbon and anise liqueur
questions.why: Orange liqueur echoes the orange in the sauce and brandy gives the flame its body; rum belongs to the Foster.

questions.q: How are the crêpes folded once they are coated in the sauce?
distractors: Rolled tightly round a sweet filling
Left flat and stacked in a pile
Folded once, pale side outward
questions.why: Folded into quarters with the first-cooked, more evenly browned side outward, they sit neatly in the pan and on the plate.

questions.q: Where did Henri Charpentier say he created crêpes Suzette in 1895?
distractors: Antoine's in New Orleans
The Savoy in London
Delmonico's restaurant in New York
questions.why: In his memoir Charpentier set the story at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, serving the Prince of Wales, later Edward VII.

questions.q: Why do food writers doubt Charpentier's account?
questions.answer: He was too young to serve a prince
distractors: Crêpes were unknown in France then
Brandy will not light in a pan
The dish was first made in New Orleans
questions.why: Charpentier was a teenage assistant waiter, and the Larousse Gastronomique doubts that he, rather than a senior waiter, served the prince.

questions.q: When do the spirits go into the Suzette pan?
distractors: Straight from the bottle into the lit pan
Before the butter and sugar melt
Over the crêpes after they are plated
questions.why: The spirit is measured into a small vessel and added off the flame, then the pan is tilted to light it; a bottle poured near a flame can catch.

questions.q: Which of these belongs to the family of flamed desserts with crêpes Suzette?
distractors: Bread pudding soufflé
Crème brûlée
Pain perdu
questions.why: Cherries jubilee, like crêpes Suzette and Bananas Foster, is a hot syrup lit with a warmed spirit at the table; crème brûlée is glazed sugar, not flamed spirit.

questions.q: A guest at Brennan's asks for crêpes Suzette. What do you offer?
distractors: Crêpes Suzette from the kitchen
The bread pudding soufflé
A plain crêpe with fresh orange juice
questions.why: Crêpes Suzette is not on the house menu; the Foster is its cousin, flamed on the guéridon at the table.
